title: Simultaneous increase of ultimate tensile strength and uniform elongation of 30Si2MnCrMoVE ultra-high strength steel by hot deformation direct quenching and partitioning
abstract: In order to further improve the combination of strength and ductility for 30Si2MnCrMoVE ultra-high strength steel (UHSS), a thermomechanical treatment, named deformation direct quenching and partitioning (DQ&P), was carried out on it. The microstructure evolutions and mechanical properties of 30Si2MnCrMoVE UHSS treated by DQ&P were compared with those treated by conventional off-line quenching and tempering (Q&T) through various microscopic characterization methods and uniaxial tensile tests. Moreover, the effects of austempering temperature on the microstructure evolutions and mechanical properties of the studied steel after DQ&P process were also investigated. The results show that the DQ&P samples, although lower or slightly lower yield strength, possess significantly higher ultimate tensile strength due to higher work-hardening rate caused by high density dislocations and fine dispersed carbides. Moreover, DQ&P310 sample exhibit apparently higher uniform elongation than Q&T sample despite of comparable content of retained austenite due to more prone to transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) effect. The DQ&P process can increase the ultimate tensile strength by 267 MPã423 MPa and the uniform elongation by 78%∼85%, respectively, as compared to Q&T process, which indicates that DQ&P process may be a promising thermomechanical treatment method to improve the comprehensive mechanical properties of the studied steel. The strengths and elongations of DQ&P samples do not vary monotonously with the increase of austempering temperature, which are both closely related to the content of retained austenite.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Quenching and partitioning (Q&P) process can obtain steels with microstructure composed of martensite and retained austenite (or ferrite, martensite and retained austenite), which have an excellent combination of strength and ductility [ 1–3 ]. During the partitioning process, carbon atoms can diffuse from supersaturated martensite to untransformed austenite, which leads to a high stability of untransformed austenite [ 4 , 5 ]. Consequently, more retained austenite can be obtained at ambient temperature, which improves the work-hardening rate and elongation of Q&P steels as it does in transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) steels [ 3 , 4 ]. In order to further improve the strength of Q&P steels, Hsu proposed the quenching-partitioning-tempering (Q-P-T) by adding some carbide forming elements such as Nb, Ti or Mo to traditional Q&P steel to introduce precipitation strengthening [ 6 ]. According to Hsu's design idea about ultra-high strength steel, Wang et al. developed a medium carbon Q-P-T steel with ultimate tensile strength over 2000 MPa and total elongation over 10% [ 7 ]. On the basis of Q&P steel, Thomas et al. proposed the non-isothermal partitioning process that would allow for the production of Q&P microstructures directly off the hot-strip mill, which proved that hot rolling might be a viable processing route for high-strength Q&P steels [ 8 ]. Afterwards, Liu et al. introduced the Q&P process into the hot stamping steel and proposed hot stamping direct Q&P process, through which the product of strength and elongation (PSE) of 22MnB5 steel was significantly improved [ 9 ]. Compared with traditional off-line Q&P heat treatment, the deformation quenching and partitioning (DQ&P, including hot-rolling or hot-stamping direct quenching and partitioning) can omit the reheating process and reduce production cost [ 8 ]. Moreover, the strain energy and deformation substructure introduced into austenite during high temperature deformation may act on the behavior of carbon atoms and ultimate mechanical properties of the steels. But up to now, the research on DQ&P has been mainly focusing on hot rolling or hot stamping of automobile steel plate [ 8–11 ]. Due to the uncontrollable billet temperature during cooling of the two processes, they are not suitable for vigorous promotion in industrial production. In contrast, the billet temperature is more controllable during the forging process due to its high flexibility. However, the application of DQ&P process in hot forging has not been reported in the published literature.

30Si2MnCrMoVE steel is a low-alloy ultra-high strength steel (UHSS), which is widely used in the field of aviation and aerospace because of its high cost performance [ 12 ]. The traditional heat treatment technology of 30Si2MnCrMoVE UHSS is off-line quenching and medium-temperature tempering (Q&T), through which good mechanical properties can be obtained (σ b  ≥ 1620 MPa,  δ 
                      5  ≥ 8%) [ 12 ]. Nowadays, the continuous progress of solid rocket motor technology puts forward requirements for large-scale and high strength parts. Therefore, the comprehensive mechanical properties of 30Si2MnCrMoVE UHSS need to be further improved to meet higher service requirements. However, previous studies have shown that the Q&P treatment can improve the ductility, but significantly reduce the yield strength and ultimate tensile strength of martensitic steels [ 4 , 13 , 14 ]. Q-P-T process can effectively increase the strength of the Q&P steels, but the addition of niobium or other precious metals will significantly raise the cost and deteriorate the hot working performance. Our previous study indicates that the DQ&P can improve the ultimate tensile strength by 224 MPa without loss of ductility of Q&P steel, but reduce the yield strength by 114 MPa, which may be due to the higher content of retained austenite [ 15 ]. Different from automotive steel, the significant reduction in yield strength of ultra-high strength steel used in aviation and aerospace is not what we expect. Therefore, it is urgent to further improve the strength of 30Si2MnCrMoVE UHSS by adjusting the content of retained austenite of DQ&P process.

In this study, in order to obtain a microstructural component with good combination of strength and ductility, the 30Si2MnCrMoVE UHSS was treated by DQ&P process with different austempering temperatures. The microstructural evolutions and mechanical properties of DQ&P samples were compared with those of sample treated by conventional Q&T process by scanning electron microscope (SEM), electron probe microanalysis (EPMA), X-ray diffraction (XRD), electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD), transmission electron microscope (TEM) and uniaxial tensile tests. Moreover, the influences of austempering temperature on the microstructure evolutions and mechanical behaviors of DQ&P samples were also investigated. The purpose of this work is to further improve the comprehensive mechanical properties of 30Si2MnCrMoVE UHSS by tuning the microstructural component.

The DQ&P workpieces were heated at 1000 °C for 30 min for complete austenitization and deformed by axial rolling, a labor-saving forming process which is illustrated in  Fig. 3 
                      a. More detailed introduction of this process can be found in Marczinski's work and Zheng et al.’s work [ 16 , 17 ]. The specific deformation parameters are listed in  Table 1 
                      . After deformation, the workpieces were immediately quenched into salt baths with temperatures of 220 °C, 250 °C, 280 °C and 310 °C and were denoted as DQ&P220, DQ&P250, DQ&P280 and DQ&P310, respectively. After that the workpieces were transferred into 400 °C salt bath for carbon partitioning for 30 s, and water quenched to room temperature. As initial state of the steels used in this study was as-forged, a secondary forging and reaustenitizing has little effect on the final microstructure and mechanical properties. The cuboid Q&T sample with a dimension of 17.6 mm × 17.6 mm × 100 mm was heated at 1000 °C for 30 min for complete austenitization, then oil quenched to room temperature and tempered at 300 °C for 3 h.

The uniaxial tensile tests were carried on Instron 8801 universal test machine (equipped with non-contact extensometer). The plate tensile specimens with a gauge dimension of 20 mm in length, 6 mm in width and 2 mm in thickness for DQ&P were taken from 1/2 thickness and 1/2 radius (1/2T, 1/2R) of the deformed disc, as shown in  Fig. 3 b. The tensile axis was parallel to the circumferential direction of the deformed disc with a draw speed of 0.6 mm/min (the initial strain rate is 5 × 10 −4  s −1 ). The temperature and equivalent strain distributions of workpieces after axial rolling were obtained by professional forging simulation software. According to  Fig. 3 c, the temperatures of tensile specimens are ranging from 940 °C to 960 °C and the effective strains are ranging from 0.8 to 1.4. The Q&T tensile specimen was taken from the heat treated cuboid with same dimensions as the DQ&P samples. Each specimen was tested three times and the average values were calculated.

The retained austenite content was measured by Brooke D8 Discover A25 X-ray diffractometer with Co  Kα  radiation (incident wavelength is 0.179 nm) at room temperature. The scanning angle was ranging from 30° to 130° with a scanning speed of 20°/50 s and a step size of 0.005°. The XRD samples were mechanically ground, polished, and then electropolished with 5% perchloric acid ethanol at 20 V for 20 s to remove the stress layer on the surface.

sections.heading: Microstructure characterization
paragraphs:
Fig. 4 
                          shows the secondary electron images of the samples treated by Q&T and DQ&P. In order to determine the microstructure composition, the secondary electron images and element distribution maps of Q&T and DQ&P310 samples were compared, as shown in  Fig. 5 
                         . It is easy to observe the uneven distribution of carbon elements in  Fig. 5 b and d, which is related to the difference in the solubility of carbon in body-centered cubic (BCC) Fe and face-centered cubic (FCC) Fe. Therefore, the brighter area with higher carbon content is retained austenite (or carbides), and the darker area with lower carbon content is martensite or bainite in  Fig. 4 . The microstructure of Q&T sample contains mainly fine lath martensite and film inter-lath retained austenite. Partial retained austenite has decomposed obviously and is presented as remnant after 3-h tempering at 300 °C, as shown in  Fig. 4 b. The microstructures of DQ&P samples are composed of mainly blocky martensite, retained austenite and some bainite. Obviously, the lengths of martensitic blocks in DQ&P samples are much finer than those in Q&T sample, which indicates that dynamic recrystallization or partial dynamic recrystallization occurred in prior austenite after 60% axial hot deformation, which has been proved by our previous work of the hot deformation behavior of the studied steel [ 12 ]. Moreover, the sizes of blocky martensite increase significantly with the increase of austempering temperature. The carbon element distribution map in  Fig. 5 d shows that the interior of island martensite in DQ&P310 sample are carbon-depleted areas. During the high-temperature deformation of prior austenite, carbon atoms are prone to diffuse to the defects, resulting in carbon enrichment near the defects and carbon poverty far away from the defects. Martensitic transformation occurs preferentially in carbon-depleted area during austempering because of low stability [ 20 , 21 ]. With the increase of austempering temperature, the nucleation sites of martensite decrease and less austenite will remain due to lower quenching stress. Subsequently, larger blocky martensite can be obtained with higher austempering temperature. In fact, it is easy to observe from  Fig. 4 c-j that although smaller blocky martensite can be obtained at lower austempering temperature, they are more like small blocky martensite obtained by dividing a large martensite in morphology.

The inhomogeneous distribution of carbon in  Fig. 5  also indicates that carbon atoms diffuse from martensite to austenite during both Q&T and DQ&P processes. According to the XRD patterns in  Fig. 6 
                         a, the retained austenite contents and carbon contents in retained austenite in the five samples were calculated based on Eqs.  (1)–(3) , as shown in 6b and 6c. The content of retained austenite first increases with the increase of austempering temperature and then decreases at 310 °C. The influence of austempering temperature on the content of retained austenite can be summarized in three aspects. (6) , more austenite can't transform to martenite during austempering and may be obtained after second quenching for higher austempering temperature. But on the other hand, according to the thermodynamics of martensitic transformation, higher austempering temperature produces less nucleation sites of martensite, which makes the same volume of austenite obtain less carbon atoms from surrounding martensite [ 22 ]. Secondly, higher austempering temperature can promote the diffusion of carbon from martensite to untransformed austenite, which enhances the stability of untransformed austenite. Thirdly, higher austempering temperature will reduce the compressive stress caused by the volume expansion of transformation, which inhibits the martensitic transformation of untransformed austenite [ 23 , 24 ]. Therefore, the content of retained austenite does not vary monotonically with the increase of isothermal quenching temperature. Considering the error of measurement method, the content of retained austenite in Q&T sample is comparable to that of DQ&P220, DQ&P250 and DQ&P310 samples, but significantly lower than that of DQ&P280 sample. The carbon content of retained austenite does not vary obviously in the whole range of austempering temperature. Moreover, the carbon content of retained austenite in Q&T sample is similar to that in DQ&P samples, taking the measurement error into consideration. The calculated dislocation densities of martensite of Q&T and DQ&P samples according to Eq.  (4)  and Eq.  (5)  are shown in  Fig. 6 d. The dislocation densities of DQ&P220, DQ&P250, DQ&P280 and DQ&P310 samples are higher than that of Q&T sample. Although more dislocations can be produced in the martensite of Q&T sample during oil quenching than that in DQ&P samples during austempering in thermodynamics, the martensite in DQ&P samples can inherit more dislocations from the hot deformed parent austenite.

Fig. 7 
                         a and b shows the inverse pole figures of Q&T and DQ&P310 samples obtained by EBSD. The block lengths of DQ&P310 sample are significantly finer than those of Q&T sample, which is consistent with the SEM observation in  Fig. 5 . The coarsening martensite lath appears in both microstructures, which indicates that the interface of martensite migrated during both Q&T and DQ&P processes [ 25 ]. It is worth noting that in the same packet, martensite grains in Q&T sample are mainly concentrated in two orientations, while martensite grains in DQ&P310 samples show more random orientation. As shown in  Fig. 7 c and d, there are three parallel martensitic grains M1, M2 and M3 in morphology, but the orientations are different from each other. From the pole figures in  Fig. 7 e, M1, M2 and M3 roughly follow the K–S relationship with the adjacent austenite grain A, i.e. {110}α//{111}γ, <1–11>α//<-110>γ. According to the crystallography of martensitic transformation, there can be six martensitic variants on each {111} plane of austenite. Furthermore, if the effect of substructure produced by original austenite deformation on martensitic transformation is considered, more orientations may occur in the same martensitic packet.

Due to the high defect densities of retained austenite in DQ&P samples, a considerable amount of austenite could not be calibrated by EBSD, even if a step size of 25 nm is adopted. In order to characterize the morphology of retained austenite, the bright and dark field images of Q&T, DQ&P220, DQ&P250 and DQ&P310 samples were obtained by TEM, as shown in  Fig. 8 
                         . In morphology, most of the retained austenite in Q&T samples is presented as fine film, while the retained austenite in DQ&P samples is presented as discrete short rod or dot.

sections.heading: Mechanical behaviors
paragraphs:
The engineering stress–strain curves of Q&T and DQ&P samples are shown in  Fig. 9 
                         a, according to which the variations of strengths and elongations with austempering temperatures are also obtained, as shown in  Fig. 9 d and e. The yield strengths of DQ&P samples are ranging from 1090 MPa to 1352 MPa, lower or slightly lower than 1381 MPa of Q&T samples, while the ultimate tensile strengths of DQ&P samples are ranging from 1935 MPa to 2091 MPa, significantly higher than 1668 MPa of Q&T sample, which indicates the larger contrast between yield and ultimate tensile strength, i.e. higher work-hardening rate of DQ&P samples. According to Hall–Petch relation, the finer packet/block sizes of martensite correspond to higher yield strengths, but they only serve as a minor strengthening component in low-temperature tempered steel [ 26 , 27 ]. The yield strength depends mainly on both the amount of retained austenite and the role that carbon play in establishing the fine structure that resists dislocation motion [ 27 ]. When stretched at room temperature, retained austenite deformed prior to martensite/bainite due to its 12 slip systems (four slip surfaces, each containing 3 slip directions) and lower Peierls-Nabarro forces [ 5 ].  Fig. 9 a shows that the elastic limits of Q&T, DQ&P220, DQ&P250 and DQ&P310 samples are comparable, higher than that of DQ&P280 sample, which can be attributed to their content of retained austenite, as shown in  Fig. 6 b. With increasing strain, the DQ&P samples show significantly higher work-hardening rate than Q&T sample. The higher work-hardening rates of DQ&P samples result from the higher densities of dislocation and fine transition carbides precipitated during the quenching and partitioning process. The interaction between higher density dislocations in DQ&P samples can effectively reduce the length of the movable dislocation segment, which leads to the more obvious increase of flow stress during stretching. Moreover, the higher density dislocations produced by hot deformation in DQ&P samples provide more sites for carbides nucleation during the subsequent quenching and partitioning processes. Higher transition carbide densities in DQ&P samples can also reduce the value of  l  in Eq.  (7) , thus increasing the flow stress and the work-hardening rates [ 5 ]. Large amount of carbides in Q&T sample are over 100 nm in length after tempering at 300 °C for 3 h, as shown in  Fig. 10 
                         a. The selected area electron diffraction (SAED) shows that these carbides are mainly transition carbides ( ε  carbides). In contrast, the sizes of carbides precipitate in DQ&P220, DQ&P250 and DQ&P310 samples are ranging from 8 nm to 30 nm, as shown in 10b-10d. For DQ&P280 sample, less carbon atoms in martensitic matrix can be used to form carbides, because more diffuse to retained austenite, which leads to relatively lower work-hardening rate.

Firstly, the higher strain-hardening rates can improve the uniform elongations of DQ&P samples due to delaying necking. According to the criterion of necking, the material necks when the work hardening rate of the material is equal to the true stress, which also marks the end of the uniform extension stage, as shown in Eq. Secondly, the higher uniform elongation should be attributed to the fact that the microstructural components of DQ&P samples are more favorable for the occurrence of TRIP effect, which can effectively delay the generation of crack and the propagation of crack tip.

Tan et al.'s recent work shows that the low deformation ability of martensite leads to the low transformation rate of retained austenite during deformation in low-C low-Si Al-added hot-rolled TRIP steels [ 11 , 14 , 29 ]. Their research also shows that the introduction of bainite into martensitic matrix can improve the deformation compatibility between soft and hard phases, promote the occurrence of trip effect, and then greatly improve the comprehensive properties of TRIP steel [ 11 , 29 ]. In this work, the introduction of bainite in DQ&P samples and low-carbon blocky martensite can effectively reduce the strength contrast between soft and hard phases and coordinate interphase deformation, which promotes the TRIP effect of retained austenite. In addition, the fine martensitic grains in DQ&P samples play a role in deformation coordination more or less.  Fig. 11 
                          shows the morphologies of central fracture regions of Q&T and DQ&P samples after tensile tests. The fracture surfaces of Q&T sample in  Fig. 11 a show quasi-cleavage fracture characteristics of ultra-high strength steel, which contains obvious secondary cracks and unevenly distributed shallow dimples, while the fracture surfaces of DQ&P samples in  Fig. 11 b-f contain almost no secondary cracks, and deeper dimples, which is a typical feature of TRIP effect fracture.

Fig. 9 d and e shows that the strengths (including yield strength and ultimate tensile strength) and elongations (including uniform elongations and total elongation) of DQ&P samples do not vary monotonically with the increase of austempering temperature. The strengths first decrease and then increase with the increase of austempering temperature, and the variation laws of elongations are just the opposite, which shows a close correlation with the content of retained austenite. Note that in Q&P steel or TRIP steel, the introduction of TRIP effect through retained austenite is often accompanied by the joint decrease of yield strength and tensile strength, as shown in the works Zhang et al. [ 4 ], Qin et al. [ 13 ], and Tan et al. [ 14 ]. The introduction of TRIP effect of retained austenite can indeed improve the ductility of the studied steel, but too high content of retained austenite seems to reduce the strength significantly. Therefore, in order to ensure the high strength of DQ&P steel, the content of retained austenite must be confined within a certain range by adopting appropriate process parameters. Previous studies indicate that the retained austenite with higher carbon content, smaller size and higher hydrostatic pressure exhibits higher mechanical stability [ 23 , 24 , 30 , 31 ]. Blocky retained austenite possesses lower mechanical stability than film-like retained austenite [ 32 ].

In this study, when the steel is austempered at 310 °C, the tensile strength can be increased by 423 MPa and the uniform elongation can be increased by 75% when the yield strength is only reduced by about 50 MPa. As for DQ&P process, the content of retained austenite of the studied steel can be reasonably controlled by selecting appropriate austempering temperatures, which can obtain a good combination of strength and plasticity. The products of strength and elongation (PSE) of DQ&P samples are ranging from 21208 MPa% to 21704 MPa%, which are 47%–50% higher than 14445 MPa% of Q&T sample, as shown in  Fig. 9 f.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
In summary, the microstructures and mechanical behaviors of 30Si2MnCrMoVE UHSS treated by off-line Q&T process and on-line DQ&P processes with different austempering temperatures were studied by SEM, EPMA, XRD, EPMA, TEM and uniaxial tensile tests. The following conclusions can be drawn: 
                         
                            (1) 
                            The microstructure of 30Si2MnCrMoVE UHSS treated by DQ&P process are composed of blocky carbon-depleted martensite, bainite and short rod or point retained austenite, which is different from that treated by traditional Q&T process, mainly composed of lath martensite and film inter-lath retained austenite. The size of blocky carbon-depleted martensite increases with the increase of austempering temperature. The contents of retained austenite in DQ&P220, DQ&P250 and DQ&P310 samples are comparable to that of Q&T sample, but significantly lower than that of DQ&P280 sample. The carbon contents of retained austenite differ little in Q&T sample and all the DQ&P samples. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            High density dislocations and fine dispersed carbides make DQ&P samples possess higher work hardening rate after yielding, which also significantly improves their ultimate tensile strength by 267–423 MPa, as compared to Q&T sample. The yield strength and ultimate tensile strength of DQ&P samples show nonmonotonic increase with the increase of austempering temperature, which is closely related to the content of retained austenite. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            The uniform elongations of all DQ&P samples are 78%–85% higher than that of Q&T sample, which can be attributed to the fact that bainite and island carbon-depleted martensite introduced into the matrix can improve the deformation compatibility between soft and hard phases and promote the occurrence of TRIP effect. Moreover, the tensile fracture of DQ&P sample shows more obvious plastic fracture characteristics than that of Q&T sample, although some of them have comparable content of retained austenite with Q&T sample. 
                         
                         
                            (4) 
                            The strengths (including yield strength and ultimate tensile strength) and elongations (including uniform elongation and total elongation) of DQ&P samples both show nonmonotonic variation with the increase of austempering temperature, which is closely related to the content of retained austenite. 
                         
                         
                            (5) 
                            Different from the effect of trip effect on the properties of Q&P steel and TRIP steel, DQ&P treatment although reducing or slightly reducing the yield strength, significantly improves the ultimate tensile strength and uniform elongation of the studied steel, which indicates that the DQ&P process could be a promising thermomechanical treatment method to improve the comprehensive mechanical properties for the studied steel.
